In the school garden behind the panchayat office, Ira's row of tomato seedlings had wilted again. 'My row gets the bad sun,' she muttered. 'Nothing I plant ever grows. It's just my luck.' At home, with four cousins talking over her, nobody waited for her answers, so she had stopped giving them.
Chandrika, the older girl who helped the gardening teacher, didn't argue. She handed Ira one clay pot and a single seed. 'Just this one. You water it after school, and you mark the stick each day.'
Ira shrugged but came every afternoon. On the ninth day a green hook pushed through the soil.
She stared at it, then at the chalk marks on her stick. 'I did that,' she whispered.

qa.q: What did Chandrika hand Ira?
qa.a: One clay pot and a single seed.

qa.q: What does Ira's whisper 'I did that' show about how her belief changed?
qa.a: It shows she began to feel that her own daily watering made the seed grow, instead of seeing everything as luck.

qa.q: Why was starting with one pot a wise choice?
qa.a: One pot made the task small enough for Ira to see her own effort work, giving her a real first win instead of another failure to blame on luck.

qa.q: If Chandrika had argued that it wasn't luck, how might Ira have reacted?
qa.a: Ira might have shrugged it off as one more person not listening, since she was used to being talked over; the seed showed her instead.

grounding: Shows a child who blames luck and has learned from not being heard that effort is useless, and a small visible win that rebuilds her belief.

Class 5 note, Friday. Nitin got 11 out of 25 in the maths test and said, before I could speak, "Ma'am, you made it too hard. I'm just unlucky." He says the same about kho-kho, about his handwriting, about everything. His mother told me he spent last year in a big class where his raised hand was rarely seen. So this week I tried small wins: one sum a day, and he predicts how long it will take. On Wednesday he said four minutes and took three. He grinned. On Thursday he asked for two sums. Next step: I will show him his own chart of times, so he can see what his practice changed.
Kalyani

"The test was unfair," Oskar said, shoving his maths paper into his bag in the Stockholm classroom. "Ms Amara just doesn't like me. It doesn't matter if I try."
Amara had heard this before. She remembered Oskar's old school reports: often ignored, rarely asked. So instead of arguing, she offered something tiny. "Want to try one experiment? Practise ten times-table questions each morning this week. Just ten."
Oskar rolled his eyes but did it.
On Friday, she gave a five-question quiz on times tables. He got four right, one more than last week.
"Luck," he muttered.
"Was it? What did you do differently?"
He paused. "I practised."
"Then that's yours."
Oskar looked at the paper a moment longer, then slid it into his folder instead of his bag.

qa.a: Ten.

qa.a: It gave Oskar a small win he could see, linking his practice to his result, so he could begin to believe his effort had an impact.

qa.a: Amara seems to see it as learned from being ignored before, not laziness, so she tries to rebuild his belief rather than scold him.
